title: Functional Features: Lambdas, Higher-Order Functions, and Streams
description: How lambda expressions, higher-order functions, and stream/generator-style processing compare across the three languages.

content.heading: Python
content.body: lambda arguments: expression creates a single-expression anonymous function. Higher-order functions (functions taking/returning other functions) are natural, since functions are first-class objects; map(), filter(), and functools.reduce() are the classic functional trio, though list comprehensions often express the same logic more idiomatically. Generators (yield) provide lazy, stream-like processing of potentially large or infinite sequences.

content.heading: Java
content.body: Lambda expressions (since Java 8), (params) -> expression, implement a functional interface's single abstract method. Higher-order-function-style code is expressed through java.util.function's standard interfaces (Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier). The Stream API provides declarative, chainable, lazily-evaluated processing pipelines (filter/map/sorted/collect) directly analogous in spirit to Python's generators and comprehensions, though with a more explicit, class-based API.

content.heading: C
content.body: C has no lambda expressions and no functional interfaces. The equivalent mechanism is function pointers: a function can be passed as an argument to another function (a callback), achieving a similar higher-order-function effect, but with none of the syntactic convenience of a true inline lambda — you must define a separate, named function elsewhere and pass its address. There's no equivalent to Python's generators or Java's Streams; lazy, on-demand sequence processing must be manually implemented (e.g., with a hand-rolled iterator struct and explicit 'next' function).

content.heading: Key Differences
content.body: Python and Java both have genuine lambda syntax and rich functional-style standard library support (map/filter/reduce and comprehensions in Python; Stream API and java.util.function in Java); C has neither — only function pointers, which achieve some of the same higher-order-function flexibility but require a separate named function and none of the inline lambda convenience, generator laziness, or stream-pipeline chaining.

content.heading: When It Matters
content.body: Porting a short, inline Python lambda or Java lambda to C means writing an entire separate, named function just to pass its address — a meaningful increase in verbosity for what's a one-line construct in the other two languages.

keyPoints: Python and Java both have genuine lambda syntax and rich functional-style APIs (comprehensions/generators in Python; Streams in Java)
C has no lambdas — function pointers (passing a separate, named function's address) are the closest equivalent for higher-order functions
Neither generators (Python) nor the Stream API (Java) have a direct C equivalent — lazy sequence processing must be hand-implemented
